arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Paul Clement argued the Ninth Circuit erred on two points. He said frequent flyer benefits relate to prices, routes, and services.
Clement stated the Airline Deregulation Act leaves airline decisions to business judgment. He argued this limits state-law interference.
Justice Kagan questioned the logic of leaving ticket decisions to the airline. She noted uncertainty about whether a passenger would accept such terms.
Justice Kennedy asked if federal common law or DOT oversight offers relief. He sought alternatives to state law or no relief.

paragraphs: This case tests whether federal law blocks state-law claims for frequent flyer benefits. Airlines say federal law preempts these claims. Passengers say state law provides needed relief.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Northwest wants the Court to affirm the preemption rule. It wants to dismiss the state-law claim for frequent flyer benefits.
Ginsberg wants the Court to reject the preemption argument. It wants to allow the state-law claim for frequent flyer benefits.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Northwest argues the Airline Deregulation Act preempts state claims. It says these claims relate to airline prices, routes, and services.
Ginsberg argues the Airline Deregulation Act does not preempt state claims. It says the airline contract lacks valid consideration under state law.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked if an unreviewable termination right makes a contract illusory. She questioned what kind of bargain that creates.
Justice Sotomayor asked if absolute discretion has a limit of reasonableness. She noted a contract without substance lacks validity.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of federal preemption in airline contracts. It determines whether passengers can sue under state law for frequent flyer benefits. It shapes the balance between federal regulation and state consumer protection.
